'velut carbasa' (as over linen) is obscure, and the edition's alternative 'ut in suppliciis' was not adopted. In Homily I, 'eam' in the speech is read as the soul addressing itself ('O soul'). 'per tot errores festinamus' is rendered as a question. In Homily II, 'peccare' is read as 'pacare' (to calm), and 'Ps. XLVIII, 4' is kept as printed, though the verse is Ps. 18:15 (Vulgate). 'Matth. u, 12' is read as Matt. 11:12.

'maxima est injuria remunerator' read as 'remuneratoris'. 'Isti tales nesciunt quid noverunt' is odd as printed; translated literally. 'tamquam nles repentinus' is corrupt (perhaps 'olus', 'flos' or similar, some plant); left as [...]. 'naturali libertate passivis perversa rapiantur incursibus' seems corrupt (perhaps 'passim diversa'); rendered loosely. 'praeteras' read as 'praeferas'. Paragraph 5 ends 'Hoc ait sermo divinus:' with no quotation following; text appears defective. The clause 'ut hoc ipsum si se non humiliet... nocere se credat' is obscure (a 'non' may be missing). 'quant se contratio oberit' read as 'quantis e contrario oberit'; 'illa anilia' read as 'illa anima'; 'stuppae facila' read as 'stuppa facile'; 'socletate 8delium' read as 'societate fidelium' (edition suggests 'felicium'). 'conservari' read as 'conversari'; 'profunda Humilis' as 'profunda fluminis'; 'laeta humiliatio' read as 'apta/digna'? rendered 'as it should'. Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'saLa' for 'sata', 'falsis' read as 'falcis' [of the sickle], 'me gere' for 'mergere', 'Bennonem' for 'sermonem', 'moris' for 'mortis', 'sibi adjutorio' for 'cibi adjutorio', 'nociis' for 'noctis', 'aruit cudi' read as 'amittendi'). nodes.text: SOME HOMILIES OF SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYON.

The divine word urges us to run while we have the light, before darkness overtakes us. We have the light if we run, if we press forward the step of faith; we sit in darkness if we stop pressing forward. Let the final necessity find us ready, for it often comes upon the unready first. Let an uncertain condition lay a certain anxiety upon us; let there be a daily fear of that danger whose onset is not known. How late will the wretched soul repent of its evils, when, as the last day comes upon it, it sees itself separated from its body, when at the end everlasting night begins to grow black and dreadful for it as it closes its eyes, when it sees lying before it, empty of health and light, its unhappy fellow-soldier, its instigator and deceiver alike, with whom it left the arena of this world defeated through its own wickedness. When, already torn from it, it begins to pour out huge and empty laments over it and to say: 'Where are your passions and your desires, with which you burned impatiently until now, and with which you continually gathered what will burn? See, all those things have passed like a shadow, the delights have gone, and only disgrace and crimes have remained for ever. Woe is me! O soul, willing or unwilling, I must return to so lost a vessel, and for fleeting pleasures I must be burned along with it in fires that can never be escaped.' What [will it be] amid these things, when the relentless exactor of what was entrusted begins to drag it off to the appointed sentence, fixed by an unchangeable law, and on this side and that the dreadful faces of the infernal ministers begin to mock it and press upon it? What will it be when it begins to be parted by the officers of death through this vast air, and to be led away along paths of darkness beyond the day, and to make a journey from which there is no return through those regions where light itself fails, when that soul, a stranger everywhere, accompanied by the sad column of its own evils, sees itself falling from the world through the farthest shores of the world into that void and emptiness, and entering that great chaos which divides the region of life from that of death, and, an exile from its own nature, losing the breath of life? When, bidding a last farewell to human things, having death before it and leaving life behind it, it is dragged into that horrible depth that the eyes can scarcely reach, chained by the various crimes of avarice and malice, to receive as much punishment as the price it has lost? And so, when it has come to these places of cruel custody, where the judgment of punishments to come will already rage by the very expectation of itself, to say nothing else, grief alone will torment the soul, bereft of all comfort; thought alone will torture it in its despair; fear alone will weigh upon it in its stupor; and because there will no longer be any anxiety there about procuring food or clothing, no occupation of labouring, soldiering or doing business, no ambition for wealth or honour, the unbearable terror of rendering account will alone fill a mind emptied of all other cares, and the weight of judgment, alone and entire, will hang over its captive senses. And what when it is commanded to go back to the prison of its body and, through the resurrection, to take it up again to share its evils? What will it do when it must be presented with the foul marks of its wounds before the pure gaze of the angels, and must give account for each thing before the king of the ages? If these things were now, beyond doubt, laid open in our midst, it could not bear its guilt within itself, crushed by the shame of great confusion. What spirit will it have then, when it sees others there receiving, as the Lord bestows it, the prize of an unharmed and whole faith, the treasure of shining chastity, the fruits of mercy, the talents of justice? When, by a lot it does not deserve, it sees the last made from the first and the first from the last? the poor glorified above the rich, servants above masters? and each one, according to their merits, flooded with the light of immortality, promoted from men to the state of angels, and with a body once earthly set upon the heights of the heavenly kingdom, and enriched among the sons of majesty with the rich inheritance of God their parent; while itself, amid all this, left behind with its sins, carries away from the spectacle of others' happiness the wounds of sorrow? What after this? when it sees itself, in a pitiable condition, stripped of all consolation, cast out into the outer darkness, and, shut off from that Church of the blessed by perpetual excommunication, cut off from the very root of life? And how will a trembling and guilty speech be able to set forth this: when the flesh that cannot be atoned for, and the marrow infected with sins, begin to be pierced by the savage heats of Gehenna, and, in the manner of seething and smelting metals, the whole substance of a human being is flooded within by unquenchable burning, and bodies and souls by the devouring flames are in part consumed, in part nourished, so that amid the very balls of fire the condemned nature both gives fodder and receives increase? If perhaps that vice long sprinkled through consciences, that adulterated mixture of bronze and lead, is at some time burned out amid the seething pools of the panting whirlpool, then for those who are to pass through the fiery shallows the length of the punishment will be the greatness of the sin; crimes will supply food to the burning, and in this the command of the one who is both author and judge will remain: that the fire, as judge, should feed on but not devour the entrails subject to pain and consecrated to torments alone, but should burn to this end, that it may forever destroy; so that the work and fashioning of our body, dead in its old crimes and brought back to life for torments alone, may find no end on the very border of destruction, but its power of endurance, drained and spent, may so perish that it rises again. For that burning is not random but reasoned and penal; because it is ordered to search out guilt, it does not know how to consume substance. And because the burning, running lightly over [it] as over linen, is itself the purging, that flame pursues not so much the guilty one as the guilt; and if there is a measure to the offences, there will also be a measure to the torments. But if the excess of capital crimes has seized and wrapped up the whole nature alike, then, because the case admits no remedy, the punishment will have no end. And so, with the penalty killing and the sentence giving life, the matter, ever renewable, will stand for ages, and will never reach the goal of its evils, since the end keeps fleeing; and since it can promise itself no hope even after immeasurable times, the torments of the ages to come will be felt already in the present; and thus immortality will increase the pain of death laid upon the conscience. Woe to those who now count as laughable what will later have to be mourned! Woe to those for whom these things must be experienced before they are believed! Therefore, dearest brothers, all these things which cannot be ended there can be redeemed here, by amendment of our former life, by almsgiving, by tears, by humility of heart, by chastity of body, by the exercise of justice and mercy. Since this is so, [why] do we, who have received so many ways to salvation, hasten to death through so many errors? Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

We ought to know, dearest brothers, what health holy occupations bring even in the present. Sacred Scripture has taught that the animals that chew the cud are clean. And what it is to chew the cud the divine word plainly teaches, saying: 'His will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night' (Ps. 1:2); and again: 'The meditation of my heart is always in your sight' (Ps. 48:4); so we too, while we spiritually chew the food of salvation, shut our senses and exclude wicked thoughts; then we delight in the praises of God, and we feel our inner self become a clean animal through holy exercises; and while we fortify our inner parts against reprobate wills, we fill our souls with heavenly food, so that the prophetic saying may be said of us too: 'He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.' The bread of angels is Christ, whose food we too share when we occupy our mind in his praises. Behold the true food, which refreshes and does not fail, but increases with use and grows by being spent. By this bread we are refreshed by hungering and fed by fasting, doing a certain violence to our vices and desires, so that it may be said of us: 'The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it' (Matt. 11:12). We ought to know who the violent are. We know that the human mind, softened by the various allurements and desires of the world, flees labour and seeks pleasure, and is scarcely brought to shut out from itself the habit of its former life; but when it begins to think on the necessity of the last day, roused and spurred by the weight of the judgment to come, either by hope of reward or by fear of punishment, it declares a voluntary war on the passions, does violence to its former pursuits, and strives to conquer itself forcibly by changing to a better life. For it cannot happen without violence that one should pass from abundance and riches to hunger and thirst, to abstinence and the cross; that one should wear down with contrition and vigils the flesh that was formerly a friend to sleep and leisure; it cannot happen, I say, without violence, that each one should exchange anger for patience, pride for humility, overcome affluence by love of poverty and sufficiency, commend sobriety in place of drunkenness and chastity in place of lust, and that a man should suddenly be transformed into another man, and in a way be rendered one from another; and thus the heavenly kingdom is seized by such people through violence. Now there are two kinds of abstinence and of the cross: one bodily, the other spiritual. The one is to refrain from drink and feasting, to restrain the appetite of the palate from delights and the softest pleasures, and manfully to call back and forcibly withdraw the senses from the things that deceive through touch, taste and sight. The other kind of abstinence and of the cross is precious and sublime: to rule the movements of the mind, to calm its disturbances with the tranquillity of moderation, to rein in the onsets of pride like a wild beast, to fight daily against one's vices, to rebuke oneself with a certain censorial severity of virtue, and in a way to join battle with the inner man. This is what he does who, having broken through the wall of the passions, climbs by violence to the kingdoms of heaven. May he deign to lead you there, living in his fear, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

The divine word instructs and exhorts us how we ought to gird ourselves to seek out its promises and to obtain those good things which can neither be grasped by sight, nor perceived by hearing, nor comprehended by thought. Ask, it says, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you (Luke 11:9). That is, that we should ask by praying, seek by labouring; that we should knock by desiring, knock by making progress, knock by persevering; and that we should be stirred towards the hope of the heavenly promises with such zeal, and burn with such longing, that the greatness of our desires may match the worth of the rewards. Our God does not want his good things to become cheap through too great an ease of finding them; a precious and desirable reward requires an eager lover and a greedy merchant.

Therefore he who promises such great gifts does not want anyone lukewarm in his work; he despises the disdainful, refuses the one who is compelled, rejects the undevoted. For to seek the grace of the divine gift slowly and with little gratitude is the greatest injury to the Rewarder. Therefore, though we sweat with all the labours of soul and body, though we exercise ourselves with all the strength of obedience, we shall still be unable to repay and offer anything of equal merit for the heavenly goods. The services of the present life cannot be set against the joys of eternal life. Though our limbs grow weary with vigils, though our faces grow pale with fasting, yet the sufferings of this time will not be worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us (Rom. 8:18). Let us knock, then, dearest brothers, as much as we can, because we cannot as much as we ought. Future blessedness can be acquired; it cannot be valued. For unless we do God's works with eagerness, with good will, with joy, let us know that we are lost to God. Do we think, dearest brothers, that that soul seeks worthily, and so knocks that it is opened to it, which at a slight command of an elder presumes to answer back and say: 'Are we your slaves? I have already done my turn; let him do his'? How does he say this, who has been commanded, 'Do not seek the things that are your own'? And again: 'Each of you not considering the things that are his own' (Phil. 2:4); from whom it is asked not only that he fulfil his own wage, but that he should take on, seize first, and snatch up the wages of others. Do we think, I say, that he so asks that he receives, so seeks that he finds, so knocks that it is opened to him, who, when rebuked for some negligence and chastised for the order of discipline, does not turn himself to amendment, nor to making satisfaction, but rather to such insolence that he says: 'I am leaving and going away; I will not put up with this; I am a freeborn man'? Now first of all, whoever boasts before the prior or abbot that he is freeborn, I think does not yet know that he has been bought. He who, bound over to Christian service, presumes to call himself freeborn, all but denies that he was purchased with the blood of Christ. What else is 'I am free' than to cry out to the Lord himself, 'I owe nothing'? Of such men the Apostle said: For when you were slaves of disobedience, you were free of righteousness (Rom. 6:20). He is not properly proved freeborn who is weighed down by the slavery of vices. Yet he cries out, in contempt of discipline, in the sin of his soul: 'I would rather leave than amend, than make satisfaction, than fulfil what you command.' What is this but to shake off the yoke of Christ from oneself with a rebellious neck? Such men do not know what they know; they have forgotten why they came here. Such men do not ask well, but are badly assailed by vices. They do not knock with faith, but are knocked about by unbelief. What good is it that you leave, you who are bound on every side by the chains of the passions, whom your vices besiege on this side and that? What good is it, I say, that you leave, who, to whatever place you go, carry yourself with you? You would rightly leave if you could flee yourself to anywhere. Someone would rightly leave if he could go where the devil could not find him. Let no one deceive himself: let him flee the adversary not from place to place, but from vice to virtue, from passion to amendment. For if you flee him in that way, he will follow you. Amend yourself, and he will flee from you, as the Apostle says: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7). Not to obey and to want to leave is to do the devil's will twice over: it is to bring damnation on oneself voluntarily even in the present. For those very ones who offend more gravely among us we can find no sadder, no harsher sentence than that, cut off from the body of the community, they should depart without peace. And is it not a kind of madness that anyone should seek as a remedy what cannot be inflicted even by the prior except for the gravest crime? Let us understand, then, dearest brothers, that these indignities and contradictions come about through the working and arranging of the enemy. For since he cannot outright drive anyone from the place of salvation, he first sends in occasions and causes; he sends in the passion of disobedience, which unbelief always accompanies as its companion. When this has ensnared the captive mind, it at once makes intolerable and impossible even those things that are small and light. And indeed there is no doubt that strength is withdrawn by God from the disobedient; just as from him who did not have in himself the necessary devotion of faith even what he had was taken away, so disobedience hardens the mind it has once seized, so that it is not bent to accept commands either by authority or by reason. But, what is worst, he trusts himself alone, follows his own intentions in place of all reason, and thinks that alone right which he has conceived with a hardened heart, becoming like him of whom the divine word declares: The ways of fools are right in their own sight (Prov. 16:25); and again: There are ways which seem to men to be right, but their ends will come to the depth of hell (Prov. 14:12). Finally, it will happen to such souls as to the house that was built upon sand (Matt. 7:26). For this parable looks especially to the disobedient. For so we read: Everyone who hears these words and does not do them will be likened to a foolish man who built his house upon sand: the floods came, and so on (ibid.); that is, when the droppings of the passions have flowed in, when the floods of the torrent and the onrush of tribulations have come from a multitude of negligences, when the winds have blown, those indeed that fly about in this air, ready to winnow Christ's threshing-floor, in case they find chaff anywhere which they may seize and scatter for their sport, then they will rush upon that house which was built without the foundation of obedience, and its ruin will be great. But perhaps someone may say: 'Is leaving this place at once to be called ruin?' I say, dearest brothers: it is no great hope if a ship set among the waves, even though it does not itself perish, yet suffers the greatest loss of its cargo and its goods, and itself arrives at port empty and void; so it is no great joy if someone, returning to the waves of the world, seems to keep the name and habit of his profession, while his soul wastes away and drains off through negligences. And what is more grievous than that you should suddenly, like a sudden [...], be uprooted from the place to which your Lord had called you, in which he had first enlightened you, into which, after the evils of the world, he had brought you as into a port out of a heavy storm? To forget suddenly brotherhood, fellowship and consolation; to forget that place in which you first put off your former habit and worldly name? Birds themselves love their nests; wild beasts love the places in which they were reared, love their lairs and pastures; and however much, by natural freedom, they are carried off in roving, scattered forays, yet they often return to the places dear to them out of a certain desire for food; and you, endowed with understanding, furnished with reason, sometimes become so out of your mind that you prefer your own wishes or intentions to the benefits of God, and follow your own thoughts, which, however much they drag you to hard labours, however much to shipwrecks of salvation and losses of the soul, yet through excessive unworthiness of heart you feel none of this. This the divine word says: For at the time of departure the enemy promises much; the man persuades himself that where he is heading he will find greater progress, much favour and an abundance of all things, and that he will be received like an angel. And after this, when he is filled with anxiety and stripped of peace, remembering how he abandoned the pursuit of his progress and the holy sheepfold, then he takes notice, and, as if the storm of his time had calmed, then he sees what evil he has done to himself, then he recognises what danger he incurred when he left without peace and with scandal the place to which he had come with joy. Then with late repentance he repents and weeps over his ruins, like certain birds which are said to weep for grief over those they have killed; and all these losses of the soul come from the evil of disobedience. But obedient and humble souls overthrow many tribulations and all labours, and cut them short. For it must be known that the more humble and obedient we are, the lighter and sweeter we shall feel the Lord's yoke upon us; the more obedient we are to our priors and fathers, so much does God hearken to our prayers. Let us see how acceptable to the Lord are the works or fasts of those who comply with their own wills rather than those of their elders. They cry out: Why have we fasted, and you did not know? We humbled our souls, and you did not look? And he answers: Because in the days of your fasts your own wills are found (Isa. 58:3). We see that through disobedience the works of souls are not regarded, their fasts not heard, their vows not accepted. Therefore let us follow the more closely the commands of him who came down to us from heaven for this, not only to redeem us by the price of death but also to build us up by the example of life; and let us say with him: I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father (John 6:38). To go after one's own wills is so ruinous that the Lord, now angered, inflicts it afterwards as the condemnation of sin, saying: And I let them go according to the desires of their heart (Ps. 80:13). Wherefore whoever wants his works to be safe and right in God's sight, let him prefer nothing to obedience, let him put absolutely nothing before it, whether he is senior or junior. Rather, the more senior he is, the more he ought to strive for edification and perfection. Let him set himself no end of progressing, and fix no limit to acquiring, when he hears it said to him: Prepare your works at the end; and again: Do not be afraid to be justified until death (Ecclus. 18:22). And again: Wisdom will be sung at the end (Prov. 1:20). So the more we progress, the more let us be humbled, because the more we are humbled, the more we shall progress. Let no senior there appear so learned as to think that obedience does not befit him, which befitted God. For humility and obedience are still a necessity in juniors, but in seniors a dignity; for he progresses well, he finishes well, who daily acts as if he were always beginning. Therefore increases of merit ought to be incentives to progress. Scripture, speaking of those who, while they pass over their first negligences, always fall into others and still others, says: The sinner will add to sinning (Ecclus. 3:29). But of progress it is said: And let the holy be sanctified still (Rev. 22:11). Let us see first what 'the sinner will add to sinning' is. For example, the passion of some evil or of detraction has begun to attack me; if remorse for this life does not bite me at once, tomorrow such an ease in this vice will come upon me, and a certain sweetness (so to speak), that I cannot call myself back from it and restrain myself. For so it happens that whoever would not amend at first begins later neither to will nor to be able. For instance, I have begun to give in to pride, I have broken the rule, I have hurt an elder, I have pulled down a junior. If I do not at once repent of having been so gravely overtaken, then from day to day the very violence of habit and the onrush of passion will carry me off most willingly, so that I no longer understand that I offend nor feel that I sin. For the burden of the offence, the constancy of offending, darkens and buries the understanding; and indeed the heart is so hardened by negligences that, if he does not humble himself, if he does not make satisfaction to his prior, he believes this very thing does harm, and moreover he gloats and says: 'How firmly I resisted him, how well I did not give in, with what authority I answered! He thought I ought always to humble myself to him.' Whoever does this has clearly handed himself over as a captive to the devil, who rejoices in the vices and passions and perdition of men; and upon such a soul will come that sentence: The sinner will add to sinning (Ecclus. 3:29). Fleeing this, dearest brothers, let us rather hold to the one that says: And let the holy be sanctified still (Rev. 22:11); let us add daily to our merits, and presume nothing of ourselves, because all that we are able to do is God's. So let us be unfailing, brothers, in the work of God, for the sake of the eternal reward, and daily strive towards better things. For the very eagerness to lay hold, the very habit of progressing, will always call us on to greater things; and where God sees a more ardent devotion of mind, he will instil affection; and as much as we add to our zeal, so much will he add to his help; as much as we apply to diligence, so much will he add to glory. To him who has it will be given, and he will have abundance (Matt. 13:12); and in another place he says: I have laid help upon one who is mighty (Ps. 88:20). So grace is born of grace, and progress serves progress; gains make gain for gains, and merits for merits; so that the more anyone begins to acquire, the more he strives and delights to seek, so that the gain of acquisition feeds the appetite for acquiring. And the more eagerly anyone has drunk of the goods of wisdom, the more he desires to drink, as Wisdom herself says of herself: He who eats me will hunger still. So let us press on with our course, dearest brothers, that our life may grow at the last. Let us seek until the end that whereby we may deserve to rejoice without end. But granted that we cannot practise bodily labours, let us turn ourselves to the desire for spiritual goods, to the increase of compunction and charity. If daily we set ascents in our hearts, we can be wearied by no infirmity, by no age, so that by these spiritual steps, as it were, we may deserve to ascend to the promises of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Just as the Lord, because of the duty of the office we have taken up, demands of us the office of speaking, so, dearest brothers, he requires of you a readiness to listen. It is as much to your advantage, I say, to obey what we say for your salvation as it is our obligation not to keep silent. For if we fear giving offence by silence, how much more ought you to dread the same offence through contempt? If, I say, it is a great danger for us not to rebuke the faults of others, how much more dangerous is it not to correct one's own? The blessed Apostle says in one place: See your calling, brothers (1 Cor. 1:26). Therefore, most beloved, let us also see our calling. For it is not enough that we have sought out this place, if here we are such as we could have been in the world. For if we look at it well, it is not only this solitude that binds us to the necessity of perfection, but also the very size of the congregation. For just as it is precious and outstanding to act well in the midst of many, and by the example of good works to rouse very many to progress, so it is dangerous and ruinous, by acting too negligently and lukewarmly, to break the faith of many and corrupt the souls of many. Just as, I say, it is fruitful to live commendably when placed in the midst of so many, so it is dangerous to have done anything that destroys. Why do I say this? Because (what is worse) we more easily find those who follow what is worse than those who follow what is better; for human frailty is more prone to imitate evil. Therefore let us not believe it sufficient for us that we see ourselves gathered into this school, since the perfection we have professed condemns our negligences in us more severely than it would if it had not been taken up. For according to the witness of Scripture, of those who promise much, much must be required. O how many the advantage of this place and the opportunity of a fitting dwelling will profit, and how many, on the contrary, it will harm! For it is not having lived in this place, but having acted well in this place, that is worthy of praise. For what does the seclusion of this dwelling profit, when malice reigns in us with tyrannical lordship, when anger rides over us, when a human eye sees more fear in us than the divine eye does; when we, those praiseworthy hermits, believe ourselves to be outside the world, yet through the vices of various passions keep the world shut up within us, so that we who thought we could aid the world itself by our prayers almost come to see that we stand more in need of the world's intercessions? For there is no doubt that the soul which, through desire for worldly pleasures, becomes a possession of worldly conduct cannot become the kingdom of the Godhead. And therefore, brothers, see your calling. To come to the desert is indeed the highest perfection; but not to live perfectly in the desert is the highest damnation. What does it profit if a quiet place is held only in body, and restlessness churns in the heart? What, I say, does it profit if there is silence in the dwelling, and in the dwellers a tumult of vices and a struggle of passions? If calm holds our outer parts, and a storm our inner? For we did not come together to this place so that the world might wait on us, so that, abounding in all things, we might enjoy every quiet; certainly not for rest, not for security, but for battle have we come together here; we have gone forth to the contest, we have hastened to wage wars against the vices: that we may blunt the swords of the tongue, and not only not inflict injuries on one another, but not even feel those inflicted. And this belongs more particularly to our profession: to seek in this life no consolation, no quiet; not to wish to receive good things in one's lifetime, but to flee honours, to rejoice in subjection and abasement, to seek poverty eagerly, and to root out from our hearts not only possessions but desires themselves. For to have nothing is sometimes a matter of necessity; but to desire nothing is a matter of virtue. And therefore the religious man ought specially to impose this measure on himself, that he have only as much as necessity demands, not as much as desire craves. For the love of having, unless it is cut out entirely, burns more fiercely over small things, and men are more tormented over the least things; and unless you are poor in heart and affection, poverty itself is to be judged not a virtue but a misery. Let us know, then, brothers, that it profits nothing if we afflict our flesh with fasts and vigils and do not amend our mind, or do not care for what is within. For what does bodily affliction profit if we pollute the tongue with wickedness and disparagement? Are not all our labours brought to nothing? Does not our work vanish like smoke and shadow, and is it not brought to nothing as easily as tow? O how great and how long-lasting labours suddenly perish! How many good things, often already acquired and laid up, are snatched from our hand, while we neglect to guard what we strive to acquire! Therefore we flatter ourselves in vain about the cross and the affliction of the body, if our outer man is exercised in holy labours and the inner man is not cured of the passions. It is as if someone made a statue golden outside and clay inside; or as if a house built with magnificent art appeared painted outside with the most beautiful colours, and inside were full of serpents and scorpions. What does it profit that you afflict your body, when your heart makes no progress? It is a very hard and most lamentable condition to spend the effort of labour with all one's intent and receive no fruit after the labour; to fast and keep vigil and not correct one's ways. It is as if someone were to clear and cultivate outside the vineyard or around the vineyard, and leave the vineyard itself deserted and uncultivated, so that it sprouts thorns and thistles, which, if the cultivator had kept at it, could have brought forth the most pleasant fruits. Recognise, then, dearest brothers, that for gaining eternal salvation bodily abstinence alone is not enough, unless the fast of the soul too, through abstinence from vices, has been joined to it. For what use is it if someone is chaste in body and polluted in mind? He whom malice corrupts, whom the fury of wrath drives about with its torches, whom pride strips of all the grace of God, whom the tongue stains with lies or curses, does he not deceive himself, does he not mock and cheat himself, if he believes he is to be sanctified by fasts and vigils alone? And therefore, most beloved, let us so exercise the body with fasts that we cleanse the mind of vices. Let us think unceasingly of the coming of that Judge, who, would that he may find us as ready as no one can doubt that he will come. And if you ask how he will come? Certainly in that body which was taken up for our salvation, handed over for our crimes, condemned for our acquittal, and pierced with lance and nails as medicine for our wounds. For the first, unbearable sentence against the guilty will be the presence of those awesome scars. What then shall we do at that time, when, over against those bruises of the crucified Lord, the marks of our sins and the stains of our lusts are brought forward? Or with what face do you think our redemption will look upon our perdition? Human offences will be the heavier, the greater the divine benefits have shown themselves. And it is to be feared that, even at his judgement, he may bring forth to the vessels of iniquity that utterance of the resurrection which testified to the precious marks of the cross, and say: Put your finger here, and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side (John 20:27), and acknowledge what I endured for you and from you, human impiety. Those marks of the nails, saving for the good, terrible for the wicked, which are not effaced until the day of judgement, are without doubt kept to be held up against them; and what follows after this but that dreadful chaos set between the living and the dead, a vast divide, the outer darkness shut out from the nature of the living, a harsh separation from the sweet sight of the saints and from the fellowship of the faithful; and on the other side, amid the tearful groans and laments of the mourners, the sad company of the wretched, and an eternal exile from the blessed homeland in the foulest night? How mournful it will be for a man to see God and lose him, and to perish before the sight of the one who was his price! And therefore, dearest brothers, thinking on these things while there is time, let us labour with unwearied zeal, so that what he conferred on us when he was judged, he may find whole in us when he comes to judge.

We know indeed that a great reward is laid up for the future for the spiritual warfare to which we have bound ourselves. But if we look well, in the very work we are doing we in a way possess even now a part of the reward; and plainly it is a great fruit of life to have been able to despise the world and to have begun to serve God; to have escaped the most unhappy lordship of the vices, and to have fled the foulest slavery of gluttony and lust. What then? Is it not already a great part of the reward to have nothing in common with the world, not to be tormented by desires for vain things, not to be mixed up in crimes, and to spend the day in innocence, to devote oneself to blessed chastity, to possess the sufficiency of glorious poverty with the fear of the Lord? Of which Wisdom speaks: Better is a small portion with the fear of the Lord than great treasures without fear. Let us understand, then, how much the Lord has conferred on us by his holy calling; let us count, if we can, from the time we seem to have been living here, how much we have gained; from how many frauds, how many adulteries, robberies, perjuries, sacrileges we have been set free; and then we shall see how much we owe the Lord even for present benefits. If we were now in the world, what else would we be doing but wallowing in our evils, violating our souls with daily stains, being pierced with daily wounds, and that without even feeling it? For the unhappy habit of sinning has this about it, that the more anyone has sinned, the less he perceives his sins, and the more sinning delights him; so that what the prophet cries out to sinners comes about: God is not before his eyes; your judgements are taken away from his sight (Ps. 9:26). For when the delight of sinning creeps in, forgetfulness at once hides the day of the coming judgement. On the other hand, the more careful anyone is about himself, the more he fears; as Scripture says: The wise man by fearing turns aside from evil (Eccl. 1:16). The wise man, therefore, is always in compunction and always in fear; and as he sighs over past evils, so he trembles with watchful care at future dangers. He who is anxious about the past thinks and turns over within himself whether perhaps he has wept too little over the past; whether perhaps he has not yet made satisfaction for his countless debts; whether perhaps he has rather laid new wounds on top of his old iniquities; whether on the old stains of conscience he has stamped fresh crimes as well, and has taken up the name of the religious life only to sin more gravely under a sacred profession. Some of us think it enough for us that we have climbed up to this retreat, that we have changed place and habit, that we have lived here a little while, placing all our hope in the number of years. And so, deceiving ourselves with a ruinous persuasion, we think we have settled all our debts, we think our evils have vanished with the passage of time; and because we have forgotten them, we believe they have slipped from the memory of the divine severity. But it is not so. All things are gathered up with him, all are laid up and sealed with him. Let us hear what is said by the one who fought hand to hand in single combat with the devil himself, blessed Job: You have sealed up my sins as in a bag (Job 14:17); and again the Lord himself says: Are not these things gathered up and sealed in my treasuries (Deut. 32:34)? Let us not think that crimes once branded in, and impressed with a deep wound in the very inward parts of the soul, can be so easily remitted. There is need of much weeping, much groaning, much sorrow of heart to heal the sorrows of that same heart. We must apply ourselves with complete contrition of spirit, so that old evils may be driven out of the conscience like arrows. It is not enough to say with the lips' edge: I have sinned, spare me, forgive. Saul too said, I have sinned (1 Kgs 26:21), but he did not obtain that pardon which David earned with a single word of penitence. And why is this? Because bare words rather than true groans expressed that confession; because the humiliation of the suppliant did not, as it should, match the greatness of the crime. It is not with light contrition that those debts are to be redeemed to which eternal death is owed; nor is passing satisfaction what is needed for those evils on account of which eternal fire is prepared. If we want to understand how grave our Judge holds the faults of men, let us look at the punishments. For as patient as our God now is in bearing our offences, so severe will he be in examining them; and just as he has prepared an inestimable glory for the just, so he has prepared an inestimable punishment for the wicked. Let us therefore infer the bitterness of the punishments, conversely, from the greatness of the rewards themselves. For he who knows how to reward merits knows how to punish offences. Most wholesome, then, and very necessary is the remembrance of the coming judgement, and the recollection, or lamenting, of past offences. And if there is anyone who flatters himself on the merits of an unharmed past life, and thinks he passed into the Lord's service still innocent, and therefore has believed he ought to be secure, let such a man consider how uncertain and slippery are the outcomes of life, of which it is said: Do not praise a man in his lifetime (Ecclus. 11:30); and when he has considered this, even if he thinks he has nothing to mourn in the past, he will find he has something to fear in the future. Let no one, then, be secure on account of the past. So many snares are laid before the feet of our soul, such countless enemies watch and guard our road, so many pits and so many precipices, so many difficulties lie between us and our end; the very road, which in itself is narrow and steep, is beset with so many ambushes of spiritual robbers; we must pass and face so many rocks and so many waves before we set our anchor on the longed-for shore; and do we think we ought to be secure on account of the past, and ought to spend our day without daily care, without daily fear and trembling? Who, crossing over the depths of some river by the narrowness of a very slender bridge, even if he has got across the greater part with untroubled foot, would believe he has already escaped the danger, when at the last stretch of the bridge, if he stumbles a little, he meets the fall he feared in the middle? So we too, even if a great part of this life seems to have passed prosperously, should not therefore presume confidence, while the last part still threatens danger. Who, placed in the battle line, would lay down his arms before the end of the fight or before the security of victory? Let no one, then, judge that he ought to be secure before he arrives at the end by a happy completion. Nor let us think this enough for full salvation, that we are reckoned among the servants of God by dwelling or counted among them by name; that we seem to live on an island and to be of standing among monks. For our God cries out to us: Not all who say to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 7:21). Why so? Because it is not the hearers of the law who are just before God, but the doers of the law will be justified (James 1:22; Rom. 2:13). Hence, even if we have lived well, we must commend our course by stability and perseverance, by persisting and making progress in the place of our calling. I tell you truly, even if we had spent twenty or thirty years here for the Lord, to whom we know we owe the whole of our life, and then spent even one year in the world, it would be beyond reckoning how much we would cheat ourselves of the joys of eternal life. For all our hopes rest in the completion and the end. What does it profit me if the crops, greening in the blade, show me the hope of harvest, and then, at the very time of the sickle, a sudden foul turn of the weather or a flood of rain cheats me? What will it profit me if the vine promises every hope in its flower, and then either the inroad of wild beasts or the havoc of hail takes away all hope just before it is fulfilled? And so all prosperity, and all [the fruit] of labours, rests in the end. And since we must grieve for those who are drawn away from here by some desires after many campaigns of labour, after some years of progress, what will become of those who think four or five years here a very long time, and spend the whole stretch of the rest of their life in the vanity of the world? For even one year in the world can so swallow up our labours won in the desert, as if the great sea were to take in a very small stream, absorb it, and leave it not even its name. I do not know for what gains we would wish to live in that world. For while here it is thought a great loss not to gain something every day, there it must be thought a great profit merely not to lose what has been gained: where, I say, it is reckoned a heavy loss not to make progress every day, there the highest virtue is not to perish. Therefore, if we are still slender and poor, let us labour to gain something here. But if we have gained something, let us take care to keep it here. This alone would be our gain and our joy, that we have lived here for the Lord. Therefore, as long as we remain here, it is in our power to turn aside to the world when we will. But once you have turned aside, it will be difficult and almost impossible even to look back in thought to this place. But if anyone thinks himself safe to leave this place at some time because he has run well here, because he has laboured much here, such a man is acting like someone who casts off from harbour a ship laden with goods, hands it over to the storms, and steers it onto the reefs and rocks. So the more we labour, the more cautious we ought to be. For the enemy lies in wait for those who make progress, and where he sees some hope, some grace, there, like a roaring lion going about, he throws himself wholly into attacking his prey; and since he cannot prevail to harm those set here, he wants to draw some of the less cautious, through thoughts and various temptations, out of this place, as it were outside the camp, and to bring them down as if from a most strongly fortified citadel, and when he has brought them down, to fight against them as if from higher ground: so that, even if he cannot sink the ship, he may at least carry off a most delightful plunder from the losses and damages that abound in the world. First he will send in various strivings, resentments, animosities: so that, while a man strives to carry out what he has once resolved and fixed upon in his fury, he does not consider his loss, does not look to his ruin; and when [the enemy] has brought him down, then there follows a repentance that will now be of no avail. We are here, and yet we are not wholly here. For either we are tossed by various wicked and shameful thoughts of the heart, or we are wounded by the poisoned swords of the tongue, taking offence over the least and smallest things, sometimes even (which does not befit a monk) breaking out into quarrels and brawls; sometimes we violate our profession by transgressing the rule, not fearing to commit theft against our priors, or rather against our own souls, under the eyes of God: what we are afraid to do in the presence of our priors, we do not fear to commit under the eyes of God; we are not content with necessities, but, through the lukewarmness of our heart, we again desire the abundance which we left behind in the world. Hence it is of little use that we have shut out whatever means we had, when the very cravings have settled down within us. That is why we are sometimes stirred up over the smallest things, and out of appetite for worthless things we stir up the most worthless strivings. Why so? Because, although we have left outward goods in [the form of] things, we still keep the inward evils in our hearts; and amid this, how our adversary exults when he sees that we have despised the greatest things only to be defeated more shamefully in the least! Therefore it profits nothing to have cast away what was placed outside, unless what has clung within, to the very entrails of the soul, is also torn out by the roots. Hence the Apostle too did not say that gold or silver is the root of all evils, but rather the desire for riches (1 Tim. 6:10); and not only the rich, but also those who wish to become rich, fall into a snare and temptation (1 Tim. 6:9). So the Apostle pursues not only those who have, but the very will to have. Therefore a man who keeps vices within himself gains nothing by leaving what is outside himself. And so (as I said), brothers, we are here, and we are not wholly here; and if we who are set within the walls scarcely hold out, what shall we do when exposed in the world? How will they be able to stand in the waves, and in the very onset of the warring storms, who are in such grave danger in the harbour? Therefore, as far as we can, let us be stable in this most tranquil bay; however negligent, however lukewarm he may be, he has not run in vain who by persevering has reached the palm of completion.

We have come together to this place, brothers, so that we may be free for our Lord, not for those things in which our enemy delights. It is certain that when we talk of the things that belong to the world, or bite one another with excessive grumbling and disparagement, he rejoices that our hours are withdrawn from God and gained for himself. What does it profit that we wear ourselves out with precious vigils and labours, and do not have what our God most desires? That is, a heart clean and free from these petty negligences: whoever does not watch for these slips away little by little and falls into greater ones. Let us therefore strive above all to have what our Lord expects in us, that is, gentle and kindly speech, a mind free from all evil-speaking, from all malice, and, avoiding those things by which the Holy Spirit is offended, giving our effort to humility, quiet, and charity: these are the chief sacrifices, these the rich burnt offerings, which rise up in the sight of the Lord as a sweet odour. Let us also strive above all that what we do in honour of our Lord we do with a bright spirit, with the joy of faith, and with the good disposition of a devoted will. But whatever we do unwillingly and under compulsion, let us know that from it we not only have no fruit, but incur very great loss. Let us suppose that someone pays homage to a powerful man, which persons of higher rank are certainly accustomed to expect from their clients: if that man saw us showing him the service due to him with an unwilling and forced spirit, even with a certain distaste, would he not rather judge that an injury had been done to him, and declare that he was dishonoured rather than honoured, and believe that such a negligent and undevoted man deserved displeasure rather than thanks in return? If, then, the service and honour of a man require devotion, faithfulness, cheerfulness, where indeed the one by whom the service is shown is sometimes better than the one who is served, where the dutiful attention itself gains no fruit, but this alone is the fruit, if he deserves to be called one received [into favour], how much more ought we to take care, in the honour of our God, not to come to his service undevoted and compelled, not sad, not ungrateful and unwilling, lest God should not regard gifts that are offered with a negligent and mean spirit? For our faith has promised that it will serve not a man, but rather him whom to serve even unto death, or to have spent life itself for, ought to seem little; to whose service and benefits even the angels themselves confess themselves unequal. And finally, though everything is owed to him, yet we pay nothing for nothing, but he, as if himself become a debtor in turn, gives a reward for the payment of debts, and for small things will repay immense ones. For in return for this wretched life, full of labours and sorrows, in which the use is short and the shortness itself uncertain, which life, even if the devotion of the will neglects to offer it to its author, the law of death will at once exact from us, and what is not given from a vow is paid from a debt: for this life, then, he will give that life which can neither be seen by the eye nor reached by the silent thought of the mind. Which indeed is easier to attain than to describe; whose course will be without end, its use without weariness, its refreshment without the help of food, its rest without the idleness of night, its age without old age, an unfailing brightness before the face of God, and amid ancient and everlasting joys an ever new delight, a secure happiness without any danger of losing it. Let us therefore try, even in this body, to have a foretaste of the sweetness of this life of those future ages by thinking of it daily even now, and, having shut out from our senses the bitterness of worldly conversations or desires, let us draw towards us with our whole hearts something of the fragrance of that blessedness; and, shaking off all torpor, all sloth, whose mother is unbelief, let us serve our Lord and God with that cheerfulness, that eagerness, and that joy with which we would come to his gifts when he himself invites us.

Those who have resolved to spend their life among many are either diligent or negligent with great fruit or with great danger; hence happy is that soul which, while it conducts itself well in the community, is the joy of many, and very many are either edified or enlightened by it. For its good things are increased while many share in them. To this too the saying of that Wise Man looks: Son, if you are wise, [you will be wise] for yourself and for your neighbours (Prov. 9:12). So if, placed in the community, he has kept obedience, if he has shown himself humble and patient, he has lent at interest to as many as he has edified; and as much good as he has lent from himself to his neighbours, so much has he turned to his own gain. But if on the contrary through his disobedience or pride he has driven others (which tends to happen more easily) to a stain, he incurs the danger of damnation for as many as he has destroyed; for as many as he has been a loss to, for so many has he contracted losses; and the sin that once went forth from him has flowed back upon him many times over. Therefore, just as he is greatly to be admired and praised whose course is the progress of many, so he is rightly to be mourned whose life is the ruin of many. And so, dearest brothers, placed as we are in the midst [of others], let us be eager to do the things that pertain to edification, so that our vices may not harm the virtues of others, so that our lukewarmness may not weaken the fervour of others, so that our anger may not violate the patience of others, so that our pride may not corrupt the humility of others, so that our weakness may not spoil the health of others, so that our foulness may not defile the beauty of others, so that we may not put out the burning lamps of others if we cannot light our own. And indeed those foolish virgins, foolish as they were, did not wish to put out the lamps of others, but to light their own. Therefore, after their likeness, if any of us lacks the richest grace, if [he lacks] the fire of kindness or of faith, the flame of fervour, the oil of charity, the light of discernment, let him come to those whom he has seen to abound more, and let him transfer his neighbour's grace to himself not by taking it away but by imitating it, and let him lay hold of the goods of another's possession without loss, indeed with gain, to the possessor. For whatever profits another from you will never be lacking to you. For a fire never felt the loss of its light when many were lit from it, nor does the multitude of those who look at it lessen the light of the sun. But to as many as look upon it, it lends its gifts, and itself always remains whole. Blessed to God is that soul whose humility confounds another's pride, whose patience puts out a neighbour's anger, whose obedience silently rebukes another's sloth, whose fervour rouses the inertia of another's lukewarmness. He who illumines the eye of his neighbour's heart, troubled by anger, with the grace of consolation and edification, is better than the one who, when a brother has been a little saddened by someone, not only does not lift him up with outstretched hand, but rather, as he totters, helps him to ruin like a leaning wall by the push of evil talk; and him who has been corrected for the sake of discipline he so incites with perverse counsels as to dash him down, so arms as to destroy him. Therefore, brothers, he for whom his own evils are not enough acts in such a way that he incurs judgement also for another's perdition. It is certain, dearest brothers, that unless we cut back and circumcise our passions here daily, we become much worse than we were while we lived in the world, so that our last state is worse than our first.

When a labourer of the earth and tiller of the country prepares his field for seed, he does not think it enough for him to have broken the rough field with the ploughshare, and to have tamed the hard clods with constant ploughing, and worked them over with frequent furrows, but in addition he takes care to clear that field of barren growths, to empty it of the harmful rubble of thorns, and to tear up the tinder of stumps with the root shaken out, knowing that his land cannot bear good without being cleansed of bad growth; heeding that word which pertains to the spiritual farmer: Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow upon thorns (Jer. 4:3; Hos. 10:12). So we too, who have been made God's husbandry, who entrust the hope of our fruits not to the earth but [hold it] laid up in heaven, should not think it enough for us to tame the earth of our body with the exercise of vigils or to work it over with the labour of fasts, but first of all let us try to cleanse the mind by rooting out vices: to circumcise our habits, cut out passions, uproot pride, plant humility, dig out anger, establish patience, prune away envy, graft in goodwill, and with virtues of this kind to make the field of the heart fruitful, as with seeds of good produce. But if the flesh is worn down and the soul bears no fruit, it is just as if a field never ceased to be ploughed and yet no harvest ever appeared. Therefore if we are not cleansed within and are afflicted without, as far as I see, we take up hostilities against both. We impose so much labour on ourselves for the sake of the soul, and spend no effort on the soul itself. We have forbidden ourselves the various pleasures of the world, the varied flavours of delicacies, in which there was something of enjoyment and sweetness; and now we cannot abstain from pride, from anger, from the poisonous passions of envy, in which there is nothing but bitterness and rancour. For love of our Lord we were most strong in leaving sweet affections and dear kin; we fled the most delightful faces of our most loving parents as if we hated them. We declared war, in a way, on filial devotion itself, and now we are weak and idle at avoiding negligences and at conquering the slightest vices. In renouncing the delight of the world we sent ahead such great things, and now we think that to stop speaking evil, disparaging, being stirred against trifles, and moreover being angry at a man and taking offence, that to overcome these things is impossible and beyond human strength. But that we now give way in lesser things, we do not blame on our own vices. For we show that whatever we now do comes not from impossibility but from lukewarmness. And so, brothers, let us look back to that faith and fervour with which we began, and to adorn the practice of our religious life let us take an example at least from our beginnings: if it is dangerous not to have added something daily, how much more dangerous is it even to have fallen back from our beginnings? It is necessary, then, that spiritual fruit, that is, the amendment of conduct, should follow bodily labour. The vices that assail both [the inner and outer] man must be overcome and conquered by the labour of each. The wearing down of the flesh is of little profit if there is no care of heart and attentiveness of mind. But if only the body labours, and our spirit resists, what profit is it for the passions to be attacked by the handmaid when they are found to be at peace with the mistress? For it is lighter if sometimes the flesh alone is troubled by some attacks, for example, is disquieted by the desire of the palate and the goads of lust. For it may be that it does not come to every danger, if the mind rejects the pleasure. But if the desire of sin holds the citadel of the mind, what does it profit me if the outer man does not yet seem stained, when his better part is corrupted? For if the inner man is conquered, both are now captive. What profit is it if we wage war outside the city and suffer destruction within? And so if, as I return from vigils, the passion of disobedience, if the spirit of envy, if the habit of disparagement receives me, if furtive presumption tempts me to transgress the rule, and if I have mixed tares with the wheat, then I have scattered what I seemed to have gathered, I have given the hope of harvest to birds and beasts. And thus in one moment I have poured out the labour of a whole night, and, what is worse, I have not even perceived that I poured it out. For this is the nature of spiritual goods: although it is certain that they are acquired with the greatest labour, they perish so easily that it can scarcely be noticed; and that is why we sometimes think ourselves holy, because we reckon the gains from our labours and are unable to detect the losses that follow. O how often we incur the evil of judging, the disease of vanity and boasting, without perceiving it! How often we are scorched by the spirit of envy, or are confounded in our very being by dishonourable and obscene thoughts, and no sense of pain, no contrition of compunction, follows the receiving of the wound! But why do I speak of these hidden things, which, penetrating to the soul itself with a kind of serpent's glide, strike the unknowing and unaware with a poisoned tooth? At times we are dashed against one another in open wars of offence of our own making; we are run through by the disparagements and evil talk of our tongue, as by our own sword, when at times we are violated by vices directed even against our priors, and in the injuries done to them we in a way strike Christ the Lord himself with our fists, who said: He who despises you despises me (Luke 10:16); and no scruple of conscience, no medicine of compunction follows. But why do I look for the medicine of penitence in us? Would that sometimes, after the pardon hoped for, there were no regret! Would that those who do not regret being forestalled did not regret being humbled! Let that soul answer me which blushed to acknowledge its sin, with deadly shame, in the sight of the brothers in the way it ought to have avoided [the sin]: what will it do when it has been presented before the divine tribunal, before the assembly of the heavenly host? When it begins to be pressed on this side and that as by most vehement witnesses, surrounded by its old evils, which it would not cure through the remedy of humility and compunction while it was permitted, which, by withdrawing and hiding them from the priors, it has kept whole for the eternal examination and the eternal judge. And so he who weeps over and lays bare faults and negligences, even those reckoned small, under present guilt, should know that he has passed from eternal punishment by a short way. So if we desire that the most busy vanity of the flesh may in no way mislead and deceive us, nor the obscenity of secret and dishonourable thought, the pleasure of the silent mind, the impiety of the unguarded heart, let us first hasten to cut out from our conduct those things which are manifest, that is, the appetite of the palate, the motions of anger, the impulses of pride, swollen contradictions, shameless disparagements. For how shall we be able to foresee the enemy in secret, if we have not been able to avoid him here as he fights in open encounter? And so, dearest brothers, our warfare requires this of us, that we fight daily not against others but against ourselves, and, constantly pursuing all our enemies within ourselves, we may obtain from the Lord the palm of spiritual triumph. And indeed as long as we belonged to the world, serving in those acts and affairs at which we now blush, the adversary did not oppose us then, indeed he even agreed with us, since in our wretched and lost life he found nothing on which to exercise his envy. Our works delighted him; our crimes sufficed for him by themselves. For who would take up war with his own soldier? Who would wish to attack his own subject? Beyond all unhappiness was the life of the one whom the enemy did not deign to harm. But now, after we have renounced those pleasures, he sees his worshippers returned to the service of their former Maker, he sees in us, in a way, his idols changed into temples of God; gnashing his teeth, and like a roaring lion, as a sleepless lurker he searches out every approach for doing harm (1 Pet. 5), he directs against us battle lines of visions, bringing with him seven spirits more wicked than himself, in case he should find our house empty and vacant of spiritual goods, and be able to occupy it with his crowds, so that he may prepare a dwelling for himself in it, the vices having been sent ahead like quartermasters. And therefore, dearest brothers, he turns over a thousand devices for harming us. All the younger and the foolish he tempts either with the enticements of unseemly gluttony, or he attacks them with the goads of untamed flesh, to see whether he can pollute their senses or their honourable thoughts, and carry off an ignoble triumph from a wound to chastity. But all the better and senior ones he tries to overthrow through the evil of pride and boasting, by their very progress and their own merits: so that, while he presses upon them their length of time and their merits, he may cut away humility of heart through the most unclean vanity, and, what is dangerous, persuade a man that he pleases himself in the sight of God. And now that is a common and familiar evil, that he arms the swords of our tongue against us, that he inflames the goads of anger. And so he makes the mind drunk with various passions, that when we are angry, or disparage, or curse, we believe we harm others. But it is not so, dearest brothers; for the evil of each vice flows back upon its own author. The evil-speaker stains his own tongue, the disparager ulcerates his own heart, the angry man blinds the light of his own mind, the envious man sprinkles his own soul with the poison of spite. In this that saying of Solomon is also fulfilled: Son, if you are evil, you alone will drink up evils (Prov. 9:12). Hence therefore it comes about, most beloved, as I said, that we sometimes feel ourselves to be worse than we were in the world, because in the struggle we are instigators to evil, because in the middle of the contest we give our hands to the enemy whom we procured by this very religious life. Nor do we persevere in the fervour in which we began, but we succumb as lukewarmness overcomes us. And therefore the name of a great profession must be defended with great strength. What we promised God by coming to the desert is much, however much there may be that we hope for from God. And therefore let us shake off all sloth, all weariness of mind, and let us carry out a precious warfare with precious devotion. Let us not wait to be compelled to the service of our Lord in the manner of hirelings and slaves, nor let us be content that another should exact from us whatever we know pertains to our salvation and glory. Above all let us take care that what we must do, we do not do unwillingly. Let us neither object before the work, nor grumble during the work, nor please ourselves over the completed work, with boasting flattering us wickedly. Above all, brothers, let us examine our negligences daily with the watchful eye of the heart, and, the cloud of lukewarmness being dispersed, let us consume them before our eyes, saying that verse: I acknowledge my sin, and my offence is ever against me (Ps. 50). It is a crime that sometimes the very habit of sinning makes our sins light and cheap to us, since it is certain that we, just as we are increased by the smallest goods, so ought to feel compunction over the smallest negligences. For it is no small thing to neglect the smallest vices in the life of men. I do not know about which offences those ought to be secure who are to be judged even for sins of ignorance, and are to render account for idle words and for thoughts. I do not know which offences they ought to neglect, about which the Lord himself declares with a certain definiteness: Amen I say to you, if anyone says to his brother, Fool, he will be liable to fire (Matt. 5:22). Who amid these things could hope for any pardon, unless, as prone as man is to transgress, so rich were the mercy of our Lord to forgive? Let us look therefore, brothers, to our calling, let us walk in humility, in all patience, in all gentleness. Let us set a guard on our mouth; let fear of the coming judgement soften anger; let the thought of the last day break pride. Let us think what mourning there will be for the negligent soul departing from this body, what distress, what gloom, what darkness, when out of that number of adversaries the first to come to meet it will be conscience, surrounded by various crimes. For it, all other proofs set aside, it will be thrust before our eyes, so that both the proof may convict us and the recognition may confound us. No one will be allowed either to hide anything or to deny it, where the accuser and witness will come forth not from far off elsewhere, but from within. Therefore, so that we may infer that future confusion from the present confusion that usually happens among men, let us think: if anyone of us had his offences and secrets laid against him among us, just as they are known inwardly to the heart, I tell you truly, he could not bear the common gaze of all; and what will the unhappy soul do when it is presented with its disgraces and foulnesses before the sight of the angels? But that soul which has directed its course well, which has obeyed Christ in its elders, which has kept its profession in all things, will not fear the necessity of that last hour; but going out from the dwelling of this body it will seem to itself as if after the long darkness of prison it were brought out into light, as if it were led out of some most gloomy cave into a royal hall, as if, drawn out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs, it were clothed in beautiful and splendid garments, and placed amid the sweetness of flowers and spices to be refreshed with wonderful fragrances. Let us recall how pleasant rest is, how delightful repose, after laying down the bundle of some very heavy burden. How sweet it is, after the chains of long captivity, to have returned to one's dear homeland with liberty recovered. How precious it is, after the dangers of much sailing, to have reached the longed-for land and the desired harbour. And from these let us gather and recognise how pleasant it will be, with a good conscience as companion, to pass to true and solid joys and to the fellowship of the angels, and to ascend to that life where there will be no labours, no pains, no losses, no troubles, and, what is above every good, no sins; but eternal innocence, inviolate justice, unshaken security and everlasting happiness.

See your calling, dearest brothers (1 Cor. 1:26). To come to the desert is the highest perfection; not to live perfectly in the desert is the highest damnation. What does it profit if quiet holds the place, and restlessness turns in the heart? If there is silence in the dwelling, and in the dwellers a tumult of vices and a struggle of passions? If calm holds our exterior and storm our interior? We are accustomed to reckon our years and the spans of time in which you now live. Let not the number of days deceive you, whoever you are, which you have spent here having bodily left the world. Count that day alone as lived in which you denied your own wills, in which you resisted evil desires. Count as lived that day which you spent without any transgression of the rule; which no malice, no envy, no pride stained; which no fault of lying or perjury spattered; which did not yield to sin, which fought back against the devil. Count as lived that day which had the light of purity and holy meditation, which dark conduct did not change into night. That day, I say, add to your life, whose use has reached your soul. We are also accustomed to flatter ourselves on the constancy of bodily fasts and visible vigils, we who after vigils, and perhaps from the vigils themselves, go out to the evil of disparagement, of wordiness, of grumbling. [For] he who withdraws from the choir of those singing psalms to shameful revels and stealthy drinkings, not only by damnable transgression but also by abominable baseness, it would be much lighter if he slept with sobriety ruling. He who fasting carries about a breast loaded and weighed down with the swelling of anger and indignation; who abstains from wine, and is troubled in his senses by the bitter drunkenness of discord; who, I say, outwardly mortifies himself by a wholesome sparingness of cups, and inwardly his heart belches up the deadly venom of hatreds from infected entrails, does he not understand, already condemned in advance even in the present life, that the prophetic words are directed at him: Not such a fast have I chosen, says the Lord (Isa. 58:5); or this: For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their vines from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and a cluster of bitterness is in them (Deut. 32:32)? Thus, moreover, when the devil sometimes notices a soul empty of faith and stripped of the fear of God, he so makes the mind drunk with various passions that when we curse, or are angry, or disparage, when we do these things, we believe we harm others. But it is not so. For the evil of each vice runs back upon its own author, as the divine word says: Son, if you are evil, you alone will drink up evils (Prov. 9:12); the evil-speaker stains his own tongue, the disparager ulcerates his own heart, the angry man blinds the light of his own mind, the envious man corrupts his own soul with pestilent spite as if with a kind of rust; and as vipers are born from ulcerated parents, as, I say, the viper's offspring are said to be born by bursting their mothers' entrails, so human hearts are first torn apart by the very passions which they have conceived. Those hearts, I say, from which the serpentine brood of vices is brought forth, are themselves first violated by the monstrous fertility of the birth. Of such a birth the divine word says: Behold, he has travailed with injustice, he has conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity. His sorrow will be turned upon his head, and his iniquity will come down upon his crown (Ps. 7). Having heard these things, then, our mind, fervent in charity towards you as it ought to be, was tormented with long sorrow over the negligences of some. [But having first expressed our affection] and with some of the heat of our heart unburdened, we instruct, we admonish, and we even beseech you on your own behalf (if indeed you do not disdain to hear the affection of one instructing you), that for the future we correct our ways and amend our negligences, lest we come here afterwards not with the rod of tongue and speech, but with those blows which hardened hearts demand. Rather strive from now on to contend among yourselves in praiseworthy rivalry and at last in a better emulation. Let each of you be readier in the work of God, more fervent in prayer, more attentive in reading, purer in chastity, more sparing in sobriety, more profuse in abundance of tears, more seemly in body, more sincere in heart; milder in anger, more measured in gentleness, rarer in laughter, more fervent in compunction, more grounded in gravity, more cheerful in charity. And therefore let us chastise ourselves, let us daily render account to ourselves of our daily conduct. Let each soul address itself in the secret places of the heart and say: Let us see whether I have passed this day without sin, without envy, without disparagement and grumbling. Let us see whether today I have done anything that would pertain to my progress, to the edification of others. I think that today I pulled down that beginner; today I was disobedient to my elder, I lied, I swore falsely, I was overcome by anger or gluttony; today I laughed too much; I indulged more in food and drink, more in idleness and sleep, than was fitting; I read less, prayed less than I ought. Who will give me back this day, which I lost in vain tales? And so, brothers, let us feel compunction for all our negligences on our beds (Ps. 4), that is, in our hearts. If you do so, we indeed shall rejoice at your progress, but you will be glad at the salvation gained; you will give us [joy] for the gaining of your salvation. May his goodness grant that you so profit from our sermon that you in turn help us by your merits, and be an ornament to us in the present [life] and a protection in the future.

The divine word says in a certain place: On the days of your solemnities afflict your souls (Lev. 16:29; 23:27). Why did it say this? Because fasts and vigils and holy afflictions wear down humbled bodies, but purify stained hearts. They take strength from the limbs, but add brightness to consciences; for the crimes of pleasures are no less redeemed by contrition. Through the exercises of the hard cross the joys of the flesh, which once deceived, are punished. And so by present mortification the sentence of future death is forestalled; and while the author of the fault is humbled, the fault is consumed; and while outward affliction of voluntary severity is applied, the offence before the dreadful judgement is appeased; and a slight labour pays debts which eternal burning would scarcely have consumed. So, treating the cause of our salvation, let us do within ourselves what physicians are accustomed to do around us. If some injury or complaint is felt in the outer skin of the body, the cure of a milder remedy is applied. But if a wound is hidden in the bones, or sunk in the depths of the inner organs, the hidden force demands a harsher and more violent medicine, so that the size of the ulcer may be overcome by cautery, and pain driven out by pain. A similar method must be applied in the sickness of the inner man. If perhaps the offences are light, for example, if a man has sinned in speech, or in some blameworthy wish, if with the eye or the heart, the stains of words and thoughts must be cured by daily prayer and private [satisfaction].
