But if someone, questioning his conscience within, [finds that] he has committed some capital crime, or if he has assailed and betrayed his faith by false testimony, and violated the sacred name of truth by the rashness of perjury; if he has stained the veil or tunic of baptism, and also the beautiful all-silk [robe] of virginity, with the filth of defiled chastity; if he has slain the new man in himself by the killing of a man; if through augurs and diviners and enchanters he has handed himself over captive to the devil: these and suchlike offences cannot be fully expiated by common and moderate or secret satisfaction, but grave cases require graver and sharper and public remedies, so that he who ruined himself with the destruction of many may in like manner redeem himself with the edification of many. For a man deceives himself if, when he feels a disease burning in his marrow, he spreads a soft ointment over the surface of the body. These principal evils, then, need great roaring, groaning and a fountain of tears, and afterwards one must weep with the prophet: I roared from the groaning of my heart; every night I will wash my bed (Ps. 6). And again: But I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping (Ps. 101). Let no one despise this humility. It was a supreme king who said these things; it was a supreme king who did these things. So, just as loud cries are raised over one who is dead, so great laments must be uttered over a soul that has been extinguished; and as a bereaved mother is accustomed to lament with broken breast over the loss of her only child, so it is fitting to be afflicted over your only one, but with hope of restoration. Of this only one the prophetic word says: Rescue my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog (Ps. 21:21). Why did it say ‘only one’? Either because it is to be loved as an only one, or because it alone and by itself will render account before the heavenly tribunal, all comforts removed. So, I say, it is necessary that over this only one, pierced through by the sword of crimes, the whole weight of grief be poured out, if perhaps, revived by fountains of tears, it may be raised up by the warmth of faith. Compunction must be kindled; prayers must be strengthened by remembrance of the future judgement and helped by works of mercy. The sentence of the prophet must be heard, but heard with the ear of obedience, when he says: Accept, O king, my counsel, and redeem your sins by alms (Dan. 4:24). The example also of that man in the Gospel must be heard as though truly written for our redemption: Behold, half of my goods, Lord, I give to the poor (Luke 19:8). Concerning whom we have heard in the Gospel the Lord saying, with ineffable condescension and charity: Whoever did it to one of these least, did it to me (Matt. 25). These words commend to us the effects of alms by heavenly authority. But perhaps, when we speak of alms, narrow poverty takes fright. Not so, dearest brothers; let it rather remember that the small coins were preferred to the treasures of the rich [...] but [God] is fed by the goodwill of the giver. But I think, dearest brothers, that our Lord permitted the poor to exist in this world so that in the poor he might test the faith of the rich, or that through mercy to the poor he might have mercy on the rich, so that, with good works abounding, this opportunity for their redemption might not be lacking; so that another's need might enrich the kindly wealthy man, and each richer man might receive great gains from the needy; and by a wonderful and supreme exchange, while mercy is bestowed on the poor with temporal generosity, an eternal treasure is repaid to himself. Let us direct our actions, and whatever we can, whatever we are able, let us devote to the exercises of good will, to the pursuits of justice and mercy. Let us run while we have the light, before the darkness overtakes us (John 12:35), because in that world it will no longer be permitted to provide for amendment and redemption. As the divine word says: For there is no one in death who remembers you (Ps. 6). So, just as there no loss of merits will any longer be feared, so no remission of sins will be granted. No freedom to practise good works will be allowed there any longer. Will anyone there be able to feed the hungry, where there will be no need of eating and drinking, where neither the impious amid the flames of hell nor the pious amid the delights of paradise will need food and drink? Will it happen there that one clothes the cold, where all care for covering the body will cease; where under that cold of which the prophet says: Before the face of his cold who will stand? (Ps. 147); where he will be naked forever who here lost the wedding garment; where the wicked will be clothed with the darkness of a stained conscience, but the good with the mantle of immortality and blessedness; where merits will be garments, as [the Lord] says: Then the just will shine; and again: Let your priests be clothed with justice (Ps. 131); or that: The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing (Ps. 44)? There, then, where an eternal tunic of light will shine forth in place of the saints' bodies, there clothing never to be put off in any ages will be turned into body; there garment will pass into reward; there that angelic robe will no longer be a covering, no longer a dress, but nature. Will the miser or the tight-fisted man there be able to do good to another out of his abundance, where his desire will not find even one drop for himself in the midst of the seething lake? For he will carry nothing with him of the things he believed he had as his own (as the prophet said): For when he dies he will not take all things, nor will the glory of his house go down with him (Ps. 48:18); and he will hear amid the various torments: I was hungry, and you did not give me to eat; I was thirsty, and you did not give me to drink (Matt. 25). Let us understand what damnation it will be to have despoiled a poor man, when it is the greatest crime not to have fed him. So to him who now oppresses the lowly and needy without any thought of the future judgement, to him, I say (as someone said), The time will come when he will wish that the poor man had been left untouched by him, and that the one he hated had not been despoiled. And how intolerable will the grief be, if anyone incurs the causes of death from that by which he could have sought the joys of life? Do not, then, despise the needy man, who, though poor for himself, can make you rich. Let us therefore seize from the present world, with fervent devotion, what we can. Our days pass quickly; would that they pass well! Let us therefore seize what we can from this world, giving thanks to him who so ordered both lives that the times of labours and contests should quickly end, but the joys of honours and rewards should endure without end.

Even if we were paying the dutiful debts of our vows to martyrs of a foreign region, we would be shown to be looking after our own advantage and benefit; faith would make them ours, and, however distant their lands, the patronage we hope for would strengthen us. For such support depends on zeal, not on places; accordingly, with the household of God you merit as much intercession as you bestow veneration. So religious devotion ought rather to win strangers over to us than the negligence of irreligious lukewarmness perhaps estrange our own from us. Let us recognise, dearest brothers, a richer bounty of divine gifts towards our Church. The peoples of individual cities exult if they are fortified by the relics of even one martyr: behold, we possess peoples of martyrs. Let our land rejoice, nurse of heavenly soldiers and fruitful mother of such great virtues. Behold, the profane enemy could never have benefited it as much by service as he benefited it by the sword. For, as the feasts of this most sacred day show, as much as iniquity abounded against it, so much grace and blessing now overflows in it. We read that in Bethlehem, by Herod, while he persecuted Christ, thousands of blessed boys were slain, as the prophet says: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be consoled, because they are not (Jer. 31:15; Matt. 2:18). So this blessed mother, the illustrious homeland of triumphant warriors, rich in the merits of such great offspring, even if to the eyes of onlookers she seemed bereaved as far as tombs go, yet in no way needs consolation, nor weeps for her children: for in enviable griefs, while she lost, she gained. Confidently, then, with you, O Bethlehem, land of Judah (who suffered the savagery of Herod in the slaughter of the boys; who at one time were found worthy to offer to God a white-robed people of defenceless infancy); worthily, I say, might our Lyon contend with you, O Bethlehem, and dispute about the divine favours to each as if in conversation with you, saying thus: O Bethlehem, in the titles of our martyrs you perhaps come first in number; I [come first] in merit. Among yours there was slaughter, not confession; among mine the struggle of suffering, among yours only the opportunity and occasion of happiness. Their end enriched you with blessing, me their courage. You in the blood of little ones could see them perishing, but could not watch them contending. The innocence of the dying crowned you, me the glory of the triumphant. Yours came to the reward of the kingdom without awareness of martyrdom; but mine, afflicted with tortures, tested by punishments, baked by savage fires in the manner of a sacrifice, received in the spirit as many crowns as they underwent penalties in the body; and so, through the blows of torments and the delays of the torturers, they conquered before they were slain. You offered those who were little in years; I those who were also perfected in merits. I offered those who conquered through their tortures when they could have been endangered in faith; you offered those who could have the fruit of dying but could not fear the danger of denying. You offered a weak people, so that the sacrilegious [king] should not find Christ; I offered a robust company, by whose example Christ gained even the sacrilegious, in the saving of the persecutors' servants. Finally, by that blessed death in which Herod, while seeking only the true Child, sacrificed so many boys, one sex earned your triumph, both earned mine: my battle carried off the palm from the prince of the world even in women. My choir could have your innocents among its boys; your choir could not have my Blandina. Divine providence granted besides that in such great sacrifices of the homeland a bishop also should not be lacking. Our blessed father Pothinus, bishop of this Church, aged and full of days, is dragged to the impious interrogation, and, for the merit, we believe, of his teaching, he is joined to his flock; and after the sacrifice of the Lord's Body he is brought before the profane tribunals to offer himself to Christ as a new victim. His aged weakness, through the abuses and afflictions of the raging officers, meets so swift an end that you would understand he had been kept until that time for martyrdom alone. Happy he who, placed at the very threshold of life, owed his end not so much to nature as to glory. Here pious minds are strengthened by the example of so great a father, and they do not so much receive the prepared punishments as rush upon them. The invincible hearts of the saints exhaust upon themselves the enormities of manifold cruelty and new tortures, and conquer the intolerable weight of evils by despising it, and by feeling it obtain that they cannot feel. Fires are set beneath them, but are found to have power only to consecrate; beasts are goaded on, but their unfed ferocity marvels at its prey. Limbs torn by various kinds of torment the flames sanctify while they do not know how to feed on them, the beasts honour while they do not know how to rage. Where are those who say that veneration should not be paid to the sacred bodies of the martyrs? Behold, the savagery of bloody ferocity, which has no sense of religion, pays the service of veneration; and that which, ignorant of reason, has no discernment, nevertheless recognises, to the condemnation of the wicked, what honour is owed to the saints. And so the minister or instrument of punishment wondrously becomes a testimony of merits; and while it shows reverence to piety, it utters a silent sentence upon impiety. Since, then, dearest brothers, our Church is adorned with such great trophies of faith, the force of iniquity laboured to surpass itself by novelty of crimes. Depriving the sacred bodies of the honour of burial, they gave them to the fires, and after the death of the men they fought against humanity itself. And though the cause of their fury had already perished, they set no end to their cruelty; yet, willing or not, they were witnesses to the blessedness of those whom they envied even when dead. How is it that malice is always joined with folly? They reduced the venerable bones to ashes, as if merits could truly be consumed by flames and virtues burned up with ashes. What confused madness! To those for whom they were winning heaven they denied earth. You achieved nothing, then, with your unheard-of savagery: in vain you believed you were extinguishing the memory of those whose glory you spread. You scatter the dust of the saints in the flowing Rhône so that it may not rise again; but resurrection is not consumed by waters, since through the grace of regeneration it is celebrated even by the gift of waters. You hand over the relics to be adored to the Rhône: the force of the river does in the dissolution of the body what time does. So whatever of human substance a bird has snatched, a beast devoured, a wave swallowed, even if it is not enclosed in a tomb, is held within the bosom of the world. For the restoration of man does not consist in the condition of the earth, but in the nature of the law and in the power of the Restorer. For he himself testified with truthful mouth: I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), who lives for ever and ever. Amen.
On the holy martyrs Epipodius and Alexander.

It is indeed a great thing to offer vows at public and common solemnities, but a more excellent festival must be judged to be rejoicing in virtues that are our own nurslings. And so the cult of native martyrs and the honour of our own patrons, just as it gives a particular joy, so it demands a special affection. For if we ought to venerate foreign palms, strange victories and crowns, and triumphs from overseas with such zeal that by our services we make our own what belongs to other places, and that what is not enclosed in our tombs may be shared through our prayers, how much more fitting is it for us, at the celebration of these men, to burn with zeal and keep watch in service, to whom religion owes manifold devotion, the Church honour, the homeland love! So that, as we are kin to them by right of birth through the bosom of one parent, we may claim for ourselves a privilege of piety and grace toward them, and may approach them first with the devotion of faith, so that we, who rejoice to be their fellow citizens on earth, may deserve to have citizenship [Greek *politeuma*, Phil. 3:20; Vulgate *conversationem*] with them in heaven. So the faith of our Church celebrates the twin trophies of Epipodius and Alexander, with an interval of two or three days between them, a feast not of relics brought from elsewhere, but a feast of the inviolate monuments of our native bosom. Very many Churches of the peoples are content even with that sanctification which they have seized by touching sacred garments from angelic limbs, or the hard bonds of chains, so that what was an instrument of punishment may be a testimony of glory, and the material of sufferings may pass into a badge of merits. But we possess the illustrious gift of the blessed whole and entire; and what could suffice for the whole world, we keep enclosed especially within the bosom of this city; and we raise up twin palms of triumph, rivals of the apostolic one, to Rome, and, having our own Peter and Paul, two advocates, we vie with that sublime see. And indeed the blessed martyrs, whose precious dust is scattered everywhere through various regions for the salvation of peoples, receive full worship in whatever place from the honour paid to God in the devotion offered them, and the richer the faith with which they are celebrated, the more acceptable to them will be the grace of the celebration. But without doubt it is far more pleasing, far more delightful to them if the fervour of devotion honours them most notably there where the fury of their passion fell upon them; if sacrifices of supplication are brought to them there where they fell down as a sacrifice to God; if a posterity worthy of praise pours out vows to them there where deadly savagery poured out innocent blood; if, finally, that enemy of the Christian name sees them consecrated there where he believed them destroyed. Sweeter, I say, does service prove to them if such great blessing celebrates them there where so great a weight of tribulations raged against them; if they are invoked for aid from the place from which, at the first sign of the resurrection, they will be called forth to their reward. Since this is so, dearest brothers, for holding the faith and cultivating religion we need not wait for any lessons from far away: we are instructed by paternal teaching and admonished by domestic examples. Does not the living voice of kindred blood cry out to us, to our heart? Learn from us, it says, to gain the faith by seeking, to cultivate it by living, to keep it by dying; learn to fear sin more than the sword; learn, for the sake of life, to love justice more than life, and faith and the fear of God. What we preserved in the midst of the tribulation of war, take care that you do not lose in peace or in the security of peace. Beware lest you lose in harbour the anchor of hope and religion which we kept safe in the waves. Beware lest, if you ever see a good life subjected to afflictions, you judge it wretched. Beware lest, in the arena of the world, into which we have been sent to undergo contests, you think any happiness is to be expected. Blessedness can be prepared here; it cannot be obtained. Do not seek here what no saint, his labour completed, no confessor obtained here; do not seek here what not even Christ found here. If the world had peace, the martyrs would not have glory; if testing did not come first, the occasion of tribulation would perish. These, then, beloved brothers, are those who have passed through great tribulations, who washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 7:14). These are the fellow soldiers of those who, according to the Apostle, were stoned, were sawn apart, were tempted, died by slaughter of the sword; in want, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy (Heb. 11:37). But amid these things perhaps, dearest brothers, when the good and holy suffer such evils here, someone thinks within himself and says: It is certain that the Lord of things does not regard what is ours, neglects human affairs, does not care for earthly things. O whoever you are, since you regard the labours of the saints, why do you not regard their rewards? See, throughout the whole world, in the holy apostles and martyrs adversity made a way for happiness, ruin fought on the side of salvation, and while it shut the door of life, it opened that of glory; and while it begrudged earth to those placing their trust in God, it prepared heaven. This, then, divine providence set before the human race as an example of patience. Since this is so, he is falsely thought wretched who is not harmed in virtue. Let no one, then, in a Christian and faithful man, call poverty, the affliction of labour and the injustices of tribulation unhappiness and misery. And when these things befall the good, let us know that they are not the disadvantages of hardships but the exercises of virtues. When a worshipper of God is permitted to struggle with adversities, he is not abandoned but tested; and so the divine word says: Blessed is he who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him (James 1[:12]). So in this world, where malice prevails and iniquity rules, the poor man is afflicted, the rich man multiplies: do you call him powerful who is strong for his own death, for whom the deceptive shadow of present gains gathers the causes of eternal evils? Who would call blessed a right hand strong against its own throat? Who rightly praises a man swift in hastening to steep precipices? Who would admire the ascent of one whom he foresees will fall from the top? It is the same, if you admire someone working impious and wicked deeds by means of wealth and riches, as if you saw someone mixing poisons for himself in a cup of gold and jewels. Or do you call him happy who, faithless, obscene, greedy and bloody, because he spurns the ways of the Lord, is permitted to go by his own, offended by the narrowness of the right hand and delighted by the breadth of the left, is wrapped in disgraceful deeds, stained with crimes, defiled by plunder, and amid all this thinks himself most blessed, and is even more unhappy for this, that he does not understand that he is unhappy? What can the medicine of the heavenly commandments do for such men, since it does not heal the unwilling? Sluggish in caring for their salvation, eager for the service of death and captivity, as it is said, they rejoice in the worst things (Prov. 2:14) and are glad at their own ruin, like those who, taking perhaps deadly juices of herbs, are said to die laughing. But amid these things someone thinks to himself and says: The God of power, the God dwelling in the citadel of justice, either does not know sins if he does not condemn them, or favours sins if he omits to condemn them. First, there is no doubt that he knows all things, he who enters and fills and exceeds all things, to whose eyes all things are exposed and naked, of whom it is said: For great is the wisdom of God, and strong his power, seeing all without ceasing. There is no doubt, then, that he knows all things and is near, he who commanded you, when you pray, to enter the chamber of your conscience; who hears in the thought and hears in the heart. And that he condemns offences and crimes the warnings of the prophets, the teachings of the apostles and the oracles of the evangelists plainly testify. Meanwhile, while he sets forth grim punishment, while he threatens eternal fire, here he gives sentence, but there he reserves [it] for punishment. Here he brandishes the sword; there he will bring destruction. Why, someone says, does he not at once punish the guilty sinner? Who could bear this error of mind? He complains of God's patience, though he does not merit indulgence; the justice of the one condemning would not be perfect unless the clemency of the one reproving went before. God in his kindness instils patience in us through the whole course of the Scriptures; and what the Lord preaches in the servant, how does the servant find fault with it in the Lord? Do we not sometimes see that even the administrators of human laws, to be praised no less for moderation than for strictness, forestall the judgments demanded with many preliminary hearings and repeated edicts? Already the guilt is proven, and still [the penalty] is deferred. Thus they display emotion in severity in such a way that they do not neglect counsel in forbearance. So too our Lord does not carelessly ignore the things done on earth, but patiently waits. He examines beforehand the works and wills of men, and so judges; he weighs merit in conduct or conversion, he tempers judgment by delay. Gradually, through the delays of times, the dispenser of eternities orders human affairs. Here he threatens the blow, there he will complete the destruction. But if God did not know human affairs, who would have been a helper to the blessed martyrs in the pressing conduct of the battle? Or how would the death of the saints be precious in the sight of God (Ps. 115:15)? Or whence would the salvation of the just be from the Lord, unless they received protection in the time of tribulation? All this shows, for those fighting the wars of faith for religion and justice, the presence of the Lord waiting and protecting. Therefore let us too confidently entreat that helper and protector of martyrs to strengthen our hands too for the spiritual combat against that enemy who, if he is dreaded, must be repelled; if he is unknown, will make his way in. But he loses much of his strength if he becomes manifest to consciences, he who conquers by ambushes alone. Our fathers fought against the harshest pains; let us, on the contrary, fight against the softest pleasures. They overcame the torments of flames; let us overcome the fiery darts of vices. They, having trampled the devil, brought back spoils from death; let us beware lest we despoil Christ in the poor. They through the power of faith were spent as a victim for God; let us watch that none of us, through the wound of sin, is made a victim of the enemy. They died in punishment in their outward limbs, and we have something to kill within ourselves. And so let us practise the battles of illustrious warriors in private combat with our passions. For since we know that there is war without a persecutor, God can give martyrdom even without blood.

Some people are in the habit of asking how man and God could be mingled in Christ. They ask for an account of this mystery, which was done once, when they themselves are quite unable to give an account of the thing which happens always: how a soul is united to a body so that a man comes to be. Therefore, just as a corporeal thing and an incorporeal one are joined, and the soul is mingled with the body so that a man is made, so man was joined to God, and Christ was made. And yet, for Christ to be made, those two incorporeal things, that is, the soul and God, could be joined and mingled more easily than one incorporeal thing and another corporeal one, that is, the soul and the body, are mingled so that the person of a man may exist.
